phenomenon.name: Possession

aliases.name: Demonic possession
aliases.meaning: Possession by a malevolent spirit, in Christian and Islamic frameworks

aliases.name: Dybbuk possession
aliases.meaning: Possession by a disembodied human soul

phenomenon.subcategory: Altered state of consciousness attributed to external agency

description.summary: Possession is the cross-cultural belief and reported experience that a human body and its functions can be controlled by an external agent — a spirit, ghost, demon, deity, or ancestor — producing dramatic changes in voice, behavior, language, and apparent identity. It is documented in 74% of 488 societies surveyed in a 1969 NIMH cross-cultural study.
description.full: Possession is an altered state of consciousness, and the associated behaviors, that practitioners and witnesses attribute to the takeover of a human body by spirits, ghosts, demons, deities, or ancestors. Anthropologist Erika Bourguignon's landmark 1969 NIMH-supported cross-cultural survey identified beliefs in possession in 74% of 488 societies sampled, with the highest prevalence in the Pacific and the lowest among Native American societies. Traditions vary widely: in many African, Afro-diasporic, Hindu, and Pacific contexts possession is sought, ritualized, and integrated with healing or worship; in Christianity and much of Islam it is regarded as an unwanted attack to be addressed through exorcism; in the Jewish kabbalistic tradition the dybbuk is a disembodied soul to be expelled. Notable cases include the witch trials at Loudun (1632–1638), the Salem witch trials (1692), the Watseka Wonder (Lurancy Vennum, 1877–1878), the Roland Doe case (1949) that inspired The Exorcist, and the death of Anneliese Michel (1976) following a Catholic exorcism. Modern psychiatric frameworks classify many possession experiences under the dissociative disorders: the DSM-5 includes 'dissociative trance' and 'possession-form dissociative identity disorder' presentations, while the ICD treats possession trance as a distinct diagnosis when culturally non-normative and distressing.

etymology.origin: Latin possessio ('a holding, occupation') via Anglo-Norman; in religious contexts 'possession' translates a range of vernacular and scriptural terms (Greek daimonizesthai 'to be demonized', Hebrew dybbuk 'attachment', Arabic mass al-jinn 'touching of jinn').
etymology.meaning: A holding, occupation, or control of a person by an outside agent
etymology.first_use: Medieval Latin Christian usage; English religious texts from the 14th century onwards

features.description: Voice changes in pitch, accent, or language during episodes
Reports of writhing, contortion, or extreme rigidity during possession states
Speaking in a language the host has not learned (claimed in many traditions; rarely substantiated under controlled conditions)

features.feature: Anomalous strength or insensitivity to pain
features.description: Reports of strength or pain tolerance beyond the host's baseline

physical.morphology: Possession is a behavioral and experiential phenomenon; the host body remains anatomically unchanged, but motor, vocal, and personality presentations alter dramatically during episodes.

abilities.description: Emergence of a distinct identity claiming to be the possessing agent
Speech in apparently unknown or unintelligible languages
In ritual mediumship, the possessing entity is consulted for guidance
In demonic-possession framings, aversive reaction to crosses, holy water, or Qur'anic recitation

patterns: Onset can be sudden or gradual
Episodes often occur in ritual or stress contexts
Cultures distinguish welcome (ritual) from unwelcome (demonic) possession
Treatment frameworks range from exorcism to therapy and psychiatric care

range.description: Beliefs in and reports of possession are found in the great majority of human societies. Bourguignon's 1969 cross-cultural survey identified some form of possession belief in 74% of 488 societies, with highest prevalence in the Pacific and lowest among Native American societies.

first_recorded.source: Mesopotamian, Egyptian, Greek, and Hebrew Bible records of possession-like states

peak_activity_periods.description: Loudun possessions in France (Ursuline convent, Urbain Grandier executed 1634)
Salem witch trials in Massachusetts framed in part by alleged possession of accusers
Roland Doe case (Maryland and Missouri); inspiration for The Exorcist (1971)
Death of Anneliese Michel in Bavaria following 67 Catholic exorcism sessions; criminal conviction of priests and parents for negligent manslaughter

temporal.seasonal_patterns: No consistent seasonal pattern; episodes cluster around ritual calendars in specific traditions.

origins.cultural_roots: Possession beliefs are documented in many of the world's earliest religious traditions, from Mesopotamian and Egyptian texts to the Hebrew Bible and Greco-Roman sources, and from Vedic and early Daoist materials in Asia.
origins.earliest_accounts: Demon-driving narratives appear in Mesopotamian incantation texts and the Hebrew Bible (e.g. 1 Samuel 16, the spirit afflicting Saul). The New Testament includes multiple possession and exorcism episodes (e.g. Mark 5, the Gerasene demoniac).
origins.folklore_connections: Tightly interwoven with traditions of spirits, ancestors, jinn, demons, and deities; with healing and divination; and with witch-hunting and demonological literature in late-medieval and early-modern Europe.

timeline.event: Loudun possessions begin among Ursuline nuns in France
timeline.significance: One of the most studied early-modern possession episodes; Urbain Grandier executed 1634
timeline.source: Wikipedia: Loudun possessions; de Certeau, M. (1970)

timeline.event: Salem witch trials in Massachusetts, fuelled in part by alleged possession of young accusers
timeline.significance: Foundational American case of possession framing in legal proceedings

timeline.event: Watseka Wonder begins: Lurancy Vennum (Watseka, Illinois) reports being possessed by the deceased Mary Roff
timeline.significance: Classic American Spiritualist case studied by E. Winchester Stevens
timeline.source: Stevens, E. W. (1879), The Watseka Wonder

timeline.event: Roland Doe / Robbie Mannheim exorcism in Maryland and Missouri
timeline.significance: Inspiration for William Peter Blatty's The Exorcist (novel 1971, film 1973)

timeline.event: Erika Bourguignon's NIMH-supported cross-cultural survey reports possession beliefs in 74% of 488 societies
timeline.significance: Foundational quantitative anthropological study of possession
timeline.source: Bourguignon, E. (1973), Religion, Altered States of Consciousness, and Social Change

timeline.event: Death of Anneliese Michel in Klingenberg, Bavaria, following 67 Catholic exorcism sessions
timeline.significance: Two priests and the parents convicted of negligent manslaughter; inspired The Exorcism of Emily Rose (2005) and Requiem (2006)

timeline.event: DSM-III introduces dissociative-disorder diagnoses that overlap with possession presentations
timeline.significance: Formalises a clinical category alongside religious framings

timeline.event: DSM-5 includes possession-form presentations within dissociative identity disorder and dissociative trance disorder
timeline.significance: Recognises culturally framed possession states in mainstream psychiatry

history.modern_era: Possession remains a living religious and clinical phenomenon. The Catholic Church's revised Rite of Exorcism (De Exorcismis et Supplicationibus Quibusdam) was issued in 1999. Pentecostal and charismatic Christian movements report large numbers of deliverance ministries worldwide. In Islamic contexts, ruqya practitioners treat reported jinn possession. Across Africa and the African diaspora, possession trance remains central to religions such as Vodou, Candomblé, and Bori. In psychiatry, ICD-11 retains 'trance disorder' and 'possession trance disorder' diagnostic categories, and a substantial literature explores cultural concepts of distress.

notable.name: Loudun possessions

credibility_factors: Subsequent historical scholarship by Michel de Certeau

notable.description: Sister Jeanne des Anges and other Ursuline nuns in the Loudun convent reported demonic possession beginning in 1632. Local priest Urbain Grandier was accused, tortured, and executed in 1634. Public exorcisms continued for years. The case is among the most extensively documented possession episodes in European history.

credibility.notes: Generally interpreted by modern historians in terms of political conflict, mass hysteria, and theatricalised exorcism rather than literal possession.

sources: de Certeau, M. (1970), La possession de Loudun

notable.name: The Watseka Wonder (Lurancy Vennum)
notable.description: 13-year-old Lurancy Vennum reportedly entered prolonged trance states in which she identified as Mary Roff, a neighbour who had died in 1865. She lived with the Roff family for several months as 'Mary' before reverting and recovering.

credibility.notes: A foundational case in 19th-century American Spiritualism and in later debates over dissociative disorders.

sources: Stevens, E. W. (1879), The Watseka Wonder

notable.name: Roland Doe exorcism

location.description: Cottage City, Maryland, and St. Louis, Missouri

notable.description: A 14-year-old boy known by the pseudonyms 'Roland Doe' and 'Robbie Mannheim' was reported to have undergone Catholic exorcism in Maryland and Missouri after disturbances followed his attempts to use a Ouija board. The case became the principal inspiration for William Peter Blatty's novel The Exorcist (1971).

credibility.notes: Highly influential cultural case; widely cited as both supportive and skeptical literature exists.

sources: Allen, T. (1993), Possessed: The True Story of an Exorcism

notable.name: Anneliese Michel exorcism
notable.description: 23-year-old Anneliese Michel underwent 67 Catholic exorcism sessions over roughly ten months in 1975–1976. She died on 1 July 1976 weighing approximately 30 kg. Two priests (Ernst Alt and Arnold Renz) and her parents were convicted of negligent manslaughter in 1978. Two films — The Exorcism of Emily Rose (2005) and Requiem (2006) — drew from the case.

factors: Death and trial documented in German court records
credibility.notes: A central modern case in debates about exorcism, mental illness (epilepsy and possible psychosis), and pastoral responsibility.

audio.name: Anneliese Michel exorcism tapes
audio.description: Audio recordings of the 67 exorcism sessions performed on Anneliese Michel.
audio.analysis: Used as evidence in the German criminal trial that convicted the priests and parents of negligent manslaughter (1978).
audio.source: German court records; Wikipedia: Anneliese Michel

documentary.name: Bourguignon cross-cultural survey
documentary.description: Erika Bourguignon's survey of 488 societies, identifying possession beliefs in 74%.
documentary.analysis: Foundational quantitative anthropological reference for the cross-cultural prevalence of possession beliefs.
documentary.source: Bourguignon, E. (1973), Religion, Altered States of Consciousness, and Social Change

documentary.name: DSM-5 dissociative disorders
documentary.description: American Psychiatric Association DSM-5 inclusion of possession-form dissociative identity disorder and dissociative trance.
documentary.analysis: Clinical recognition of culturally framed possession experiences within psychiatric nosology.

paranormal.name: Demonic / spirit possession
paranormal.description: Possession is the literal takeover of a human body by a discrete supernatural agent — demon, jinn, ancestor, deity, or disembodied human soul — to be addressed through religious specialists.

scientific.name: Dissociative trance and identity phenomena
scientific.description: Possession experiences are dissociative states in which alternative identities or 'parts' emerge; in DSM-5 and ICD-11 these are recognised as dissociative identity disorder presentations and trance/possession trance disorders when culturally non-normative and distressing.
evidence_cited: Clinical course and response to psychotherapy

scientific.name: Cultural concepts of distress
scientific.description: Possession is a culturally specific idiom for expressing distress, conflict, and trauma, especially in social contexts where direct expression is constrained.
proponents: Medical anthropologists (e.g. Janice Boddy on Sudanese zar)
evidence_cited: Patterned demographics of possession (often women in patriarchal contexts)
Therapeutic and social functions of possession ritual

skeptical.name: Misdiagnosis of neurological and psychiatric conditions
skeptical.description: Many possession cases plausibly involve epilepsy, schizophrenia, dissociative disorders, Tourette syndrome, or hypoglycaemia, mistaken for supernatural agency in religious frameworks.
evidence_cited: EEG findings in cases like Anneliese Michel (epilepsy diagnoses)

skeptical.name: Suggestion, role enactment, and social reinforcement
skeptical.description: Possession episodes are shaped by expectation, suggestion, and role enactment within religious or ritual frameworks, with iatrogenic worsening in cases of repeated exorcism.
evidence_cited: Documented worsening of cases under intensive exorcism (e.g. Anneliese Michel)
Outbreak structure of possession panics in convents and schools

traditions: Roman Catholic exorcism (Rite of Exorcism, 1614; revised 1999)
Islamic ruqya and treatment of jinn possession
Afro-diasporic possession religions: Vodou, Candomblé, Santería
folklore.beliefs: Across many traditions, possession is treated as real and consequential; responses range from ritual welcome (mediumship) through containment and accommodation to forceful expulsion (exorcism).

indigenous.significance: In many of these traditions, possession is a positive ritual and healing resource rather than an attack; treatment as pathology has historically been a colonial imposition.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Care should be taken not to conflate ritual mediumship with demonic possession or to treat all possession traditions through a Christian or psychiatric lens.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Use the terminology of the tradition being described; consult community practitioners and scholars before publishing on living practices.
